segments.title: Designing a Timberborn watershed for storage and expansion
segments.body: The map places water sources in deep basins so that each spring forms a small reserve instead of draining at once. Most of the water can escape through one low outlet concealed by foliage, while narrow channels from the higher sources create smaller losses. This restriction turns an apparently resource-rich map into a storage problem: the player can eventually block the outlets, raise the water level and support a much larger settlement. The terrain retains that future capacity because the design favors a city that can keep evolving after its early problems are solved. Timberborn abstracts real hydraulics, but the map still asks the player to read a watershed, reserve capacity and plan infrastructure for later growth.

evidence.note: Deep-basin springs, restricted map outlets, and the option to impound more water later for a much larger city.

segments.summary: Springs in deep basins and a deliberately restricted outlet turn the custom map into a long-term water engineering problem.

segments.title: Why distributed resources call for a railway
segments.body: A second large Timberborn map puts timber, metal and other resources in different corners around a central settlement. Ordinary paths can connect them, but the distances make bulk transport slow and awkward. That geography motivates the desired steam-train modification, which would turn scattered deposits into one usable production system. A deposit offers little practical value when its output cannot move efficiently. The proposed railway matches the route to the distance, volume and spatial distribution of the cargo. It remains a desired modification rather than a feature of the unmodified scenario.

evidence.note: Resources in different corners of a large map motivate a desired steam-train modification for efficient transport.

segments.summary: A desired steam-train modification shows why bulk resources scattered across a large map need a transport network.

segments.title: Balancing floods, droughts and automated water gates
segments.body: The map looks easy because it contains abundant water and metal, yet too much inflow can be as dangerous as too little. High water inundates the obvious cropland, while channels of different depth make the timing and volume of drainage harder to predict. Fixed dams can preserve water for droughts, but later inflows may spill over the banks and across crops. A proposed gate modification would connect a gate to a flow meter and adjust its opening with the water level. That would let the player retain water during droughts while controlling the next inflow. On this map, the middle difficulty can be easier than the nominally easy setting, which floods. Scarce water creates the opposite incentive: players retain as much as possible and risk a flash flood when flow returns. Flood protection, drought reserves and control rules must work together even within Timberborn's simplified hydraulics.

evidence.note: Excess inflow floods cropland and storage can create flash-flood cycles, motivating the choice of water-level-controlled gates.

segments.summary: The map's apparent abundance exposes a systems problem: flood protection, drought storage and gate-control rules can undermine one another.

segments.title: Scattered resources and the cost of reaching them
segments.body: Metal deposits across the Timberborn map draw attention toward several possible expansion routes, even though one nearby area already contains enough for the settlement's needs. Their distribution is a deliberate distraction in the map design. Reaching the distant deposits requires planning access, and terrain at the same height suggests a long straight connection. A railway would make that route efficient. The scenario asks the player to consider transport effort alongside the apparent abundance of resources.

evidence.note: Scattered metal deposits encourage expansion planning despite adequate nearby supply, with a straight railway proposed for efficient access.

segments.summary: Scattered metal deposits encourage expansion plans even when nearby supply is sufficient, making access costs part of resource strategy.

segments.title: Why raising the reservoir requires more than another dam
segments.body: Raising the map's water level would reshape the whole settlement. The plan involves building around the map and probably filling low ground to bring more land up to the new level. That would mean producing soil and reaching the stage when golems are available. Extra water storage therefore depends on construction and technology elsewhere in the settlement. The larger reservoir is a possible later development whose supporting work must be planned in advance.

evidence.note: A higher water level would require building around the map and probably filling low ground, with soil production and golems needed for that work.

segments.summary: Larger water reserves would require construction around the map and probably soil production to raise the surrounding low ground.

segments.title: Reading the Western Squadron's Brest blockade
segments.body: The Western Squadron's blockade of Brest frames a reading guide to Royal Navy operations from 1793 to 1815, a span of nearly twenty-two years. Roger Knight's Convoys is recommended alongside N. A. M. Rodger's The Command of the Ocean. The recommendation presents Rodger's book as broad naval-history reading for roughly 1650 to 1850.

evidence.note: The Western Squadron and the Brest blockade of 1793-1815, with recommendations for Convoys and The Command of the Ocean. A further Brest book title is unclear in the captions.

segments.summary: A short reading guide places the Western Squadron's blockade of Brest in the wider story of Royal Navy operations from 1793 to 1815.

segments.title: Laying out roads before buildings lock the settlement in
segments.body: Before unpausing, the player maps a straight road from one side of the settlement to the other because beaver travel time depends on route length. This early network sets the geometry for later buildings and movement between the district centre and work sites. Roads are cheap to plan at the beginning and costly to reroute once structures and resource flows depend on them. Early alignments create durable constraints even when later needs change, which is the basic problem of infrastructure path dependence.

evidence.note: Establishing a straight road network before buildings avoids the time and resource cost of later changes.

segments.summary: An early road decision shows how route geometry and later construction costs make infrastructure choices difficult to reverse.

segments.title: How district-center range shapes transport access
segments.body: The early settlement needs several routes between its district center, storage and work sites. Timberborn limits tasks by their distance from that center, so nominally connected buildings may still sit beyond useful reach. Road access therefore affects how much of the map the first district can support. The game turns a simple placement decision into a transport problem defined by travel distance and administrative range.

evidence.note: Storage and additional roads placed near the district center because activity is limited by distance from it.

segments.summary: Road and storage placement must account for the limited working range measured from Timberborn's district center.

segments.title: Housing as the ceiling on Timberborn's labour force
segments.body: Housing is an early production requirement because the Folktails population grows only when adults have room to reproduce. The number of beds sets an effective population ceiling, which in turn limits how many jobs the settlement can fill. More houses can expand the labour force, but the resulting population must still have enough food and water. The other playable tribe uses breeding pods supplied with berries, so its population depends on a different production arrangement. In either case, growth depends on what the settlement can sustain.

evidence.note: Housing priorities and Folktails reproduction, compared with the other tribe's berry-fed breeding pods and the need to sustain the resulting population.

segments.summary: Early labour growth depends on housing capacity, while every additional worker also increases the settlement's food and water needs.

segments.title: Separating imperial government from field command
segments.body: A vast war effort needs political and administrative direction alongside a commander focused on campaigns. In this imagined division, Roboute Guilliman is the regent who coordinates the wider strategy while another Primarch acts as Lord Commander in the field. Jaghatai Khan suits the military role because he could organize varied formations without becoming easy for an enemy to read. The comparison with Lion El'Jonson suggests that an opponent can plan more readily against a familiar, formulaic commander than against one whose methods remain uncertain. Although the example comes from fiction, it draws a clear distinction among government, strategic coordination and operational command. Uncertainty about an adversary's methods can itself create an advantage.

evidence.note: The regent's strategic and administrative work distinguished from the Lord Commander's field role, with Jaghatai Khan's less predictable approach potentially complicating enemy planning.

segments.summary: A Warhammer 40,000 comparison separates governing a war effort from directing campaigns and uses an unfamiliar commander to illustrate strategic uncertainty.

segments.title: Guilliman's political persona and administrative image
segments.body: Roboute Guilliman's political skill includes presenting the version of himself that a situation requires. His rigid and intensely organized image may therefore be partly constructed. Signs of humor suggest a more flexible personality beneath that public role. The fictional example separates administrative competence from the persona a leader uses to project authority.

evidence.note: Guilliman as a master politician whose rigidly organized image may be partly a presentation, with his sense of humor also considered.

segments.summary: Guilliman's highly organized public image is read as part of his political skill rather than a complete picture of his character.

segments.title: Roboute Guilliman through Nimitz, Cunningham and St Vincent
segments.body: The historical comparison places Roboute Guilliman closer to Eisenhower, Nimitz, Cunningham and St Vincent than to Grant alone. The shared traits are strategic thought, bureaucracy and organization rather than personal combat prowess. Cromwell is another possible parallel because he combined military direction with political and administrative ability. A senior coordinator also needs capable operational subordinates, illustrated by Grant and Sherman or Eisenhower and Patton. The fictional comparison separates theater-level direction from the work of commanders sent to conduct particular campaigns and battles.

evidence.note: Guilliman compared with Eisenhower, Nimitz, Cunningham, St Vincent and Cromwell for strategic and administrative ability. Grant with Sherman and Eisenhower with Patton illustrate the need for operational subordinates.

segments.summary: Eisenhower, Nimitz, Cunningham and St Vincent help explain why Roboute Guilliman is a strategic coordinator rather than simply a battlefield general.

segments.title: Montgomery, MacArthur and the burden of command ego
segments.body: Putting Montgomery and MacArthur in the same command structure would make cooperation extraordinarily difficult because of their egos. In this deliberately sharp comparison, Montgomery is the more consistently competent officer, while MacArthur combines occasional brilliance with serious failures. Talent alone does not make a senior subordinate manageable: personality, authority and willingness to coordinate affect whether a coalition strategy survives contact with its commanders. The joke about placing Montgomery over MacArthur sharpens the problem of matching formal hierarchy to personal power. This narrow comparison does not attempt to evaluate every campaign led by either general.

evidence.note: Montgomery's competence and ego compared with MacArthur's flashes of brilliance, frequent incompetence, and equally difficult ego.

segments.summary: A deliberately sharp comparison separates Montgomery's competence from MacArthur's uneven record while showing how ego can damage a command system.

segments.title: Serving under MacArthur or commanding the German Navy?
segments.body: Both choices are treated as difficult, but serving as MacArthur's deputy leaves a way to take effective command. The joke is to give him food poisoning and take over while he is incapacitated. His deputy would then have a capable force to direct. A command role in the German Navy offers no comparable solution because the force itself is profoundly out of balance. Sidelining a commander cannot remove that structural weakness.

evidence.note: Preference for serving as MacArthur's deputy, with a joke about incapacitating him to take command, contrasted with the German Navy's unbalanced force.

segments.summary: A deliberately unpleasant command choice turns on the German Navy's fundamental imbalance in the Second World War.
segments.question: Would you rather be MacArthur's second-in-command or command the German Navy in the Second World War?
segments.answerShort: Serving under MacArthur is the preferred choice: his deputy could take over a capable force, whereas the German Navy would still be profoundly unbalanced.

segments.title: Why Wellington might adapt well to modern war
segments.body: Wellington might be one of the few commanders of his era able to perform competently if placed in the Second World War. The case rests on his habit of studying geography, terrain and the ground on which an army had to operate. That method could help him recognize changed conditions and adjust his decisions. The comparison judges historical commanders by transferable habits of analysis instead of carrying their old tactics unchanged into a new technological setting.

evidence.note: Wellington might adapt successfully to the Second World War through his study of geography, terrain, and topography and his ability to adjust to new parameters.

segments.summary: Wellington's close study of geography and topography becomes the basis for judging how a historical commander might adjust to modern warfare.

segments.title: Wellington's cavalry appointments and command quality
segments.body: A joke about putting MacArthur under Wellington ends with the suggestion that he might become Wellington's cavalry commander. The accompanying quip alleges that Wellington put officers he disliked in charge of cavalry because they would get themselves killed. That is offered as a humorous explanation for poor British cavalry performance in the Napoleonic Wars. The criticism concerns the effect of personal dislikes on officer selection, rather than establishing a deliberate policy of sacrificing commanders.

evidence.note: A humorous claim linking Wellington's dislike of cavalry appointees with their deaths and poor British cavalry performance, prompted by a MacArthur counterfactual.

segments.summary: A humorous MacArthur counterfactual becomes a caution about how officer selection can weaken an arm of service.

segments.title: Why hindsight would create a different Battle of Waterloo
segments.body: Wellington's quip about having won Waterloo illustrates a problem with hindsight. If a commander knew in advance where and when Napoleon would attack or when Blücher would arrive, he would deploy differently. Napoleon would then respond to the new deployment, producing a different battle from the one that supplied the hindsight. Counterfactual analysis must therefore model reactions and feedback instead of changing one decision while freezing every other actor.

evidence.note: Foreknowledge of Napoleon's attack or Blücher's arrival would alter Wellington's deployment and therefore change the battle itself.

segments.summary: Knowing Napoleon's attack plan or Blücher's arrival time would change both Wellington's deployment and the opponent's response, not simply improve the historical result.

segments.title: Earlier Greenboy shells and naval counterfactuals
segments.body: The possibility of earlier Greenboy shells shows why an alternate-history question cannot stop at one altered event. Giving the Royal Navy effective shells earlier in the First World War changes more than the immediate result of a single engagement. Better ammunition would influence later choices and generate a widening chain of operational and strategic consequences. A useful naval counterfactual must follow the responses produced by a technical change instead of holding the rest of history fixed.

evidence.note: Earlier Greenboy shells as an alternate-history premise whose improved Royal Navy shells would produce many further effects.

segments.summary: Earlier Greenboy shells offer a compact example of how one naval-technology change can reshape wider First World War choices.

segments.title: Why foreknowledge changes the future it predicts
segments.body: Foreknowledge creates a feedback problem because people act on what they learn. A forecast may describe what happens if no one intervenes or if one choice is made, but a different response produces a different path. The Alpha Legion is criticized for accepting the Cabal's vision without first asking how being told about it had already changed events. The fictional example extends the Waterloo discussion by showing why a prediction cannot be treated as fixed once it influences a decision-maker.

evidence.note: Acting on foresight changes events, prompting criticism of the Alpha Legion's acceptance of the Cabal's forecast without accounting for that feedback.

segments.summary: The Alpha Legion's faith in a forecast illustrates how receiving information can invalidate the future that information described.

segments.title: Planning ahead by securing basic needs first
segments.body: Victoria 3 rewards thinking three or four steps ahead, a demand that can catch out players accustomed to reacting to events. Timberborn illustrates the same approach when timber production is delayed until housing, population growth, water and basic food are secure. More workers are needed for later industry, and they need beds and sustenance before that production can expand. Berries, chestnuts and carrots are enough for this early stage. The immediate priority is to establish the population and its supplies before pushing into further production.

evidence.note: Reactive play compared with thinking several steps ahead, with housing, population, water, and food prioritized before timber production.

segments.summary: A comparison between Victoria 3 and Timberborn shows why strategy begins with dependency chains rather than the most visible production goal.

segments.title: Was Buçaco a British or French victory?
segments.body: Wellington was already conducting a planned withdrawal toward the Lines of Torres Vedras. At Buçaco, his smaller Anglo-Portuguese force is credited with inflicting two to three times the casualties it suffered. The battle also bought time for those defenses to be completed, which was the immediate strategic purpose. The French could claim that they continued to push the defenders back, but withdrawal was part of Wellington's plan. On that assessment, Buçaco was an Anglo-Portuguese victory despite the continued French advance.

evidence.note: An Anglo-Portuguese victory judged by the stated casualty ratio of two or three to one and by the time gained for the Lines of Torres Vedras.

segments.summary: Buçaco is assessed by casualties and by Wellington's larger aim of buying time for the Lines of Torres Vedras.
segments.question: Was the Battle of Buçaco a British victory or a French victory?
segments.answerShort: An Anglo-Portuguese victory: Wellington inflicted heavier losses and gained the time his strategy required, even though the French continued their advance.

segments.title: Can the best Napoleonic components make the best army?
segments.body: The proposed composite army includes French artillery, Portuguese and British infantry, and British logistics under Wellington and Blücher. Other armies also contain good troops, and other generals deserve consideration. There is doubt that Wellington and Blücher would make the best command partnership. Choosing an ideal army therefore requires people who can work together, even when each component looks attractive in isolation.

evidence.note: A proposed composite Napoleonic army prompts doubt about Wellington and Blücher as partners, recognition of other good troops and generals, and a requirement for people who can work together.

segments.summary: An idealized composite army still depends on whether its chosen troops and commanders can work together.
segments.question: Would combining the strongest arms, logistics and commanders from different Napoleonic armies create the ideal force?
segments.answerShort: Only if the selected people can cooperate, because individual excellence does not guarantee an effective command team.

segments.title: The Great Emu War as an operational mismatch
segments.body: The Great Emu War becomes a humorous example of armed force failing to achieve its task. Machine guns and troops in lorries fail to stop the emus going where they want. The joke depends on the gap between the equipment available and the inability to redirect the birds. Descriptions of the emus as Australia's undefeated rulers and superior strategists are comic exaggerations. The operational criticism concerns the failure to divert the animals despite the force deployed.

evidence.note: Machine guns and troops in lorries fail to divert the emus, followed by jokes about the birds outwitting the Australian Army.

segments.summary: Machine guns and lorries fail to divert the emus in a comic account of an operation that could not achieve its task.

segments.title: Buçaco in Wellington's campaign of delay and withdrawal
segments.body: Wellington's purpose at Buçaco was to gain time before falling back on the Lines of Torres Vedras. A Portuguese corps reaching a crossroads in time could have blocked Masséna and forced another battle, delaying the French further. That opportunity did not change the underlying plan: withdrawal remained the intended course unless an extraordinary victory destroyed Masséna's army. The defensive campaign aimed to strain French logistics until they broke. Orderly disengagement mattered because many of the losses that made French victories overwhelming came during the defeated army's withdrawal. Keeping an army together under those conditions required skill and some luck. Washington's repeated preservation of the Continental Army provides another example of recognizing when to pull out and retaining a force.

evidence.note: A missed opportunity to delay Masséna at a crossroads within Wellington's planned retreat to Torres Vedras. French logistics, orderly withdrawal, skill and luck, and Washington's preservation of his army explain the wider campaign argument.

segments.summary: Wellington's planned withdrawal toward Torres Vedras aimed to gain time, strain French logistics and preserve his army.

segments.title: Samuel Pepys and the work of naval administration
segments.body: Pepys's job is the preferred choice, though his work was demanding. He is admired for doing it well and for enjoying a full life. The personal reservation concerns his desire for children. He apparently never became a father, despite wanting to, and that unfulfilled wish tempers the favorable assessment.

evidence.note: Preference for Pepys's demanding but successful career, qualified by his apparently unfulfilled wish to become a father. The particular captaincy proposed in the question is unclear.

segments.summary: Samuel Pepys's demanding career is the preferred choice for its accomplishment and enjoyment, with a reservation about his unfulfilled wish for children.
segments.question: Would you prefer a captaincy or Samuel Pepys's job?
segments.answerShort: Pepys's job: it was hard work, but he was effective at it and led an unusually full and successful life.

segments.title: Why leaders must build an effective command team
segments.body: Political skill, public communication and administrative competence are separate abilities, and finding all of them in one person is difficult. A leader therefore needs capable advisers and must be willing to listen to them. Building that team is a skill in its own right because complementary abilities and conflicting personalities have to be balanced. Ordinary group projects may miss this work when teachers assign the members or friends choose one another without considering the task's full needs. Choosing friends can leave a group with duplicated abilities and missing skills, so team selection needs attention alongside teamwork itself.

evidence.note: Political, administrative, and public-speaking abilities distinguished, with adviser selection, balanced skills, and management of conflicting personalities treated as leadership skills.

segments.summary: Leaders need advisers with complementary skills and must judge whether different personalities can work together.

segments.title: Timberborn's appeal to engineering students
segments.body: Alex Clarke's engineering students introduced him to Timberborn because they enjoyed its ecological simulation. The custom map gives water management a direct role in farming. Levees help shape the land available for agriculture, and part of the map is set aside for that use. Designing the terrain lets the player create these interactions between water and food production.

evidence.note: Engineering students' enthusiasm for ecological simulation, followed by the use of levees and farming on the custom map.

segments.summary: Engineering students' interest in ecological simulation leads into an example of levees and farming on a custom Timberborn map.

segments.title: Technical possibility is not the same as sensible design
segments.body: The original Stronghold's isometric presentation is preferred here to the 3D approach of Stronghold 2 and 3. The judgment concerns enjoyment and gameplay as well as the visual change. A new technical capability does not establish that using it will produce a better game. Designers still need to ask whether the change is sensible for the experience they want to create.

evidence.note: The original Stronghold's isometric design compared with later 3D games, raising the question of whether technical possibility justifies a change.

segments.summary: The Stronghold games illustrate why a new technical capability should be judged by what it improves rather than adopted merely because it exists.

segments.title: Which Warhammer 40,000 faction has the best infrastructure?
segments.body: A clear ranking remains uncertain because the factions have different requirements. Necron infrastructure is theoretically excellent but decaying without adequate maintenance, while the Imperium possesses vast systems that often receive no upgrades. Ordinary improvements to tanks, equipment and armour should have continued regardless of the gene-seed changes associated with the Primaris project. The Tau are difficult to judge without knowing more about those who run their society. Orks need little conventional infrastructure. The Tyranids appear to be an entirely fleet-based organism, but too little is understood about them to assess their infrastructure or the full threat they pose. In this fictional comparison, inherited equipment, maintenance and continuing development need separate consideration. Uncertainty about an opponent's requirements also limits the usefulness of comparisons.

evidence.note: Decaying Necron systems, Imperial failures to improve tanks and equipment independently of gene-seed work, uncertainty about Tau leadership, Orks' limited needs, and poorly understood Tyranid infrastructure.

segments.summary: A faction comparison separates inherited technical stock from infrastructure that can be maintained, improved, understood and matched to actual needs.
segments.question: Which Warhammer 40,000 faction has the best infrastructure, and which has the worst?
segments.answerShort: There is no simple ranking: usable infrastructure depends on maintenance, upgrades, understanding and what each faction actually needs.

segments.title: Teaching no-win decisions through abstraction and history
segments.body: Star Trek's Kobayashi Maru puts the participant personally in command of a no-win scenario. That makes it difficult to admit that the situation cannot be won. The proposed teaching sequence begins with an abstract example in which the learner has no personal stake, allowing the problem to be recognized at a distance. A historical case follows, asking what a real decision-maker did under comparable constraints. Only after those examples does the learner enter a scenario without being told that it is unwinnable. The progression gives the learner a basis for recognizing the predicament before having to confront it in a command role.

evidence.note: The Kobayashi Maru's personal command problem and a proposed teaching progression from an abstract no-win scenario to a historical example and then a personally involving exercise.

segments.summary: Abstract examples, historical cases and personal command scenarios provide a staged method for learning to recognize unwinnable situations.

segments.title: Imperial xenophobia in doctrine and diplomacy in practice
segments.body: The Imperium's official xenophobia coexists with pragmatic agreements with alien groups. Those agreements do not fit the strict doctrine proclaimed on paper. The gap suggests that policy is applied more flexibly than the ideology implies. This is an interpretation of a fictional institution and its diplomacy.

evidence.note: The Imperium's formal xenophobia compared with its more pragmatic practice and numerous agreements with alien groups.

segments.summary: The Imperium's formal xenophobia sits uneasily beside the agreements its institutions make in practice.

segments.title: Building force strength for a return to the offensive
segments.body: Roboute Guilliman's tacit tolerance of chapters growing beyond the thousand-Marine limit is interpreted as a pragmatic response to military need. This is a distinction between tolerating expansion and formally changing the rule. Removing a limit would still leave formations needing time to build their strength. Replenishing existing chapters to their authorized numbers provides immediate readiness, while allowing further growth prepares capacity for later crusades. Formations away from active fronts may have more opportunity to accumulate personnel. The strategic argument is that Guilliman must eventually regain the offensive against Abaddon, whose preparations have already achieved their primary objectives. In this fictional war, changing force policy and generating the troops needed to act on it are separate tasks.

evidence.note: Tacit tolerance of larger chapters, the time needed to increase their numbers, replenishment to authorized strength, and the argument for building forces for future offensives against Abaddon.

segments.summary: Guilliman's tolerance of oversized Space Marine chapters reflects a force-generation problem: formations must grow before a state can sustain offensive action.

segments.title: Trainees as a reserve beyond formal strength limits
segments.body: A chapter can keep substantial numbers of aspirants outside its count of full Space Marines. That offers a way to remain formally compliant with chapter limits while preparing more personnel. Those trainees can become full Marines quickly when needed. In this fictional example, replacement capacity depends on the pool already in training as well as the formation's present strength.

evidence.note: Large numbers of trainees preserve formal compliance while providing personnel who can become full Marines quickly.

segments.summary: A large pool of aspirants can provide rapid replacements while a Space Marine chapter remains formally within its strength limit.

segments.title: Building research capacity before advanced infrastructure
segments.body: The settlement cannot place an underground pile on demand because research must unlock the design first. Early inventors generate science, while later observatories expand that capacity as advanced systems demand larger research reserves. Production also moves from logs to planks to gears, so knowledge and manufacturing capacity have to develop together. Advanced infrastructure therefore depends on research capacity and the workshops that supply its components.

evidence.note: Advanced storage needs science from inventors and later observatories, alongside production from logs to planks and gears.

segments.summary: An underground store cannot be ordered on demand: inventors, observatories and a logs-to-planks-to-gears production chain must create the capability first.

segments.title: A proposed division of command across the Imperium
segments.body: One imagined command arrangement leaves Guilliman running the Imperium as regent while Lion El'Jonson becomes its senior military commander. Another Primarch would assist Dante, with a further one operating more freely. Jaghatai Khan is the preferred partner for Dante because the two are expected to work well together. Their partnership would repeat the division between field command and the administrative work of a regent. This is a speculative arrangement for the fictional setting, built around delegating duties and matching personalities.

evidence.note: A proposed division among Guilliman, Lion and other Primarchs, with Khan suggested as a compatible partner for Dante and command separated from administration.

segments.summary: A speculative Guilliman-Lion arrangement extends the split between administration and field command to a possible Khan-Dante partnership.
